summary: Aperture of the iris; size depends on age, light and dilating drops. A fixed mid-dilated pupil is a key sign of acute angle closure.

diameter.note: Real (anatomical) pupil in the iris plane under slit-lamp room lighting; senile miosis with age. Winn 1994 measured the entrance pupil, so its values are divided by 1.134 (optics.entrance_magnification). Clinicians see optics.entrance_diameter.

dilated_diameter.note: Real pupil after tropicamide 1%: entrance-pupil values divided by 1.134, then reduced 12% as a render choice, because the published size looked too large on screen. Render-calibrated, not clinically validated. Used when the case is examined dilated.

decentration_x.note: Pupil centre relative to the limbus centre in the iris plane; +x temporal, so negative is nasal. Low confidence.

decentration_y.note: Pupil centre relative to the limbus centre; +y up. Low confidence.

vertical_ratio.note: Vertical over horizontal pupil diameter; diameter is the horizontal one. A vertically oval pupil follows sphincter ischaemia in acute angle closure. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 9th ed.; render-calibrated (low).

entrance_magnification.note: Paraxial magnification of the iris plane by the cornea (Atchison & Smith 2000, ch. 5); about 1.135 at age 20.

entrance_diameter.note: Apparent pupil seen through the cornea: what a clinician measures with a ruler or pupillometer.

provenance.source: Winn et al., Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 35:1132 (1994) for age-related pupil size (converted to the real pupil); Yang, Thompson & Burns, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 43:2508 (2002) for decentration (low confidence); Atchison & Smith, Optics of the Human Eye (2000), ch. 5 for entrance-pupil magnification
